crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: How a paper is cited covers the paths a reference takes from one work to the next: who cites whom, in what context, and how those links accumulate into a citation graph. It sits inside citation mapping and discovery, where the unit of interest is the relationship between two papers rather than either paper alone. The scope runs from a single in-text mention through reference lists, bibliographies and indexing services to the large graphs built on top of them.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is the reference list and the full text around each mention, gathered from publishers, preprint servers and open indexes. Persistent identifiers such as DOIs anchor records, while author names, titles and venues are matched to disambiguate works that share similar metadata.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Counting citations is the simplest layer, and it is done by resolving each reference to a canonical record and tallying inbound links. Contextual citation analysis goes further, reading the sentence or passage where a citation appears to classify whether it supports, disputes, extends or merely mentions the cited work. Graph methods then trace paths, clusters and influence across the network, and text extraction pulls the specific claims a citing paper attributes to its source.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Citation data carries provenance questions, because a reference can be wrong, retracted, duplicated or padded, and because self-citation and citation cartels distort counts. Records should point back to the original paper so a reader can verify the claim at its source, and any derived metric should state which index and snapshot it came from. Rights attach to the full text and to the databases that host it, so reuse of reference lists and abstracts depends on the terms of each source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward richer, machine-readable citation records that carry context alongside the link, so a citation can be filtered by intent rather than counted blindly. Open citation initiatives and identifier standards are pushing coverage beyond the large commercial indexes, and language models are being used to summarise and classify citation contexts at scale. The open question is how much of that summarising can be trusted without a reader returning to the cited paper itself.
sections.heading: Where it is going
